title: Bali Belly vs Food Poisoning: What Is the Difference?
content:
Are they the same thing?

Not exactly, but they overlap heavily. "Bali Belly" is a traveller's nickname for diarrhoea and stomach upset during a stay in Bali, and doctors usually call it traveller's diarrhoea. "Food poisoning" describes illness caused by eating contaminated food. Many cases of Bali Belly are caused by contaminated food or water, so in practice the two often describe the same event.

## How they can differ

**Timing.** Some food poisoning, particularly from toxins already present in the food, can start within hours of a meal and settle within a day or two. Traveller's diarrhoea caused by bacteria, viruses or parasites often starts later, sometimes a day or more after exposure, and can last longer.

**Main symptoms.** Early, heavy vomiting is more typical of toxin-type food poisoning. Watery diarrhoea with cramps is the classic picture of traveller's diarrhoea. Both can cause nausea, tiredness and a low fever.

**Who else is ill.** If several people who ate the same meal become ill around the same time, food poisoning from that meal is more likely.

You cannot reliably tell the cause from symptoms alone, and it usually does not change the first steps of care.

## What to do for either

- Replace fluids with small, frequent sips of water or oral rehydration solution.
- Rest and avoid alcohol.
- Eat plain food only when your appetite returns.
- Ask a pharmacist or doctor before taking anti-diarrhoeal medicine, especially with fever or blood in the stool.
- Wash your hands carefully and avoid preparing food for others while you are unwell.

## When to see a doctor

Get assessed if you have blood in your stool or vomit, a high fever, severe or worsening abdominal pain, signs of dehydration, vomiting that stops you keeping fluids down, or symptoms that are not improving after a few days. Infants, older adults and pregnant women should be assessed early. Go to the nearest emergency room for fainting, confusion, or inability to keep any fluids down.

## Next steps

See our guide to [Bali Belly symptoms and warning signs](https://balibellyrecovery.com/symptoms.html), learn [what treatment can include](https://balibellyrecovery.com/treatment.html), or find out [how a doctor home visit works](https://balibellyrecovery.com/doctor-home-visit.html).

## Important note

This article is general information and does not replace an individual medical assessment.

title: Bali Belly and IV Drips: Do You Actually Need One?
content:
## Not everyone needs an IV drip

Bali Belly causes fluid and salt loss through diarrhoea and vomiting. In mild cases, drinking small, frequent amounts of water or oral rehydration solution is often enough, and an IV drip is not needed. Whether an IV is appropriate is a medical decision made after an assessment.

## When oral fluids are usually enough

- You can keep fluids down
- You are passing urine regularly and it is not very dark
- You are not dizzy when you stand up
- Symptoms are mild and starting to improve

## When a doctor may recommend IV fluids

A doctor may consider an IV drip when dehydration is moderate or worse, or when oral rehydration is not working, for example if you are vomiting so much that you cannot keep fluids down. The decision depends on your symptoms, how long you have been ill, your hydration, your medical history and the examination findings.

## What an IV drip does and does not do

An IV drip gives fluids and electrolytes directly into the bloodstream, which can correct dehydration faster than drinking when you cannot keep fluids down. It does not cure the infection itself. Medication such as anti-nausea treatment may be given alongside it if the doctor judges it appropriate.

## Signs you should be assessed urgently

Go to the nearest emergency room for fainting, confusion, blood in stool or vomit, severe or worsening abdominal pain, very high fever, or inability to keep any fluids down. A home visit is not a substitute for emergency care.

## What a home visit involves

Our doctor assesses you at your villa or hotel and decides what care is appropriate. That may be oral fluids and advice, medication, or an IV drip, and some patients are advised on oral fluids and other care instead. See [what treatment can include](https://balibellyrecovery.com/treatment.html), how a [doctor home visit works](https://balibellyrecovery.com/doctor-home-visit.html), and the [package options](https://balibellyrecovery.com/packages.html).

## Important note

This article is general information and does not replace an individual medical assessment.

## Introduction

Bali Belly is a common term used by travellers to describe digestive illness experienced during a trip to Bali.

## Common Symptoms

Symptoms may include diarrhoea, nausea, vomiting, stomach cramps, and abdominal discomfort.

## When to Seek Medical Help

Seek medical assessment if symptoms are severe, persistent, or accompanied by signs of dehydration, blood in the stool, or high fever.

## Important Note

This article is for general educational purposes and does not replace an individual medical consultation.

title: How Long Does Bali Belly Last? A Realistic Recovery Timeline
content:
## The short answer

Most cases of Bali Belly, which doctors usually call traveller's diarrhoea, improve within a few days, and most people feel back to normal within about a week. How long yours lasts depends on the cause, how much fluid you can keep down, and your general health.

## A typical timeline

**Day 1 to 2:** Symptoms often start suddenly with loose stools, stomach cramps, nausea, and sometimes vomiting or a mild fever. This is usually the roughest stretch.

**Day 2 to 4:** Vomiting commonly settles first. Stools may stay loose, and tiredness and low appetite can linger.

**Day 4 to 7:** Most people are clearly improving, although the stomach can stay sensitive for a few more days.

This is a general guide, not a promise. Some infections run longer, and some people recover faster.

## What helps you recover

- Drink small, frequent sips of water or oral rehydration solution. Oral rehydration salts are sold in pharmacies in Bali.
- Rest, and return to plain food such as rice, bread or bananas once your appetite comes back.
- Avoid alcohol, and avoid very oily or spicy food until you feel better.
- Ask a pharmacist or doctor before taking anti-diarrhoeal medicine, especially if you have a fever or blood in your stool.
- Do not start antibiotics on your own. They are not needed in every case, and the doctor decides whether they are appropriate.

## Signs you should not wait it out

Get a medical assessment if you notice any of the following:

- You cannot keep fluids down
- Blood in your stool or vomit
- Severe or worsening abdominal pain
- High fever, confusion or fainting
- Signs of dehydration: dizziness when standing, very dark or very little urine, a dry mouth
- Symptoms that are not improving after a few days
- Diarrhoea that lasts more than a week or two, because some parasitic infections need specific treatment

Infants, older adults, pregnant women and people with other medical conditions should be assessed early. For fainting, confusion, blood in vomit, or inability to keep any fluids down, go to the nearest emergency room.

## If you are too unwell to travel to a clinic

If you are stable but too unwell to go out, a doctor can assess you at your villa or hotel. Read how a [doctor home visit works](https://balibellyrecovery.com/doctor-home-visit.html), check the [areas we cover](https://balibellyrecovery.com/covered-areas.html), or review the full list of [symptoms and warning signs](https://balibellyrecovery.com/symptoms.html).

## Important note

This article is general information and does not replace an individual medical assessment.

title: How to Avoid Bali Belly: Practical Food and Water Tips
content:
## You can lower the risk, not remove it

Even careful travellers get Bali Belly sometimes. The tips below reduce your exposure to the contaminated food and water that cause most cases.

## Water

- Drink sealed bottled water or water that has been properly treated.
- Use the same water for brushing your teeth.
- Be cautious with ice when you are unsure where it came from. If in doubt, ask or skip it.
- Keep your mouth closed in the shower and when swimming in pools or the sea where water quality is unknown.

## Food

- Choose food that is freshly cooked and served hot.
- Be careful with raw or undercooked meat, seafood and eggs.
- Be cautious with salads and raw vegetables. Fruit you peel yourself is generally safer.
- Avoid food that has been sitting out at warm temperatures, such as buffets or street stalls without turnover.
- A busy place with fast turnover is usually a better sign than an empty one, but it is not a guarantee.

## Hygiene

- Wash your hands with soap and water before eating, and after using the toilet.
- Carry hand sanitiser for times when soap is not available.
- Do not share utensils or drinks when someone in your group is unwell.

## Before you travel

Ask a travel doctor or clinic about vaccinations that may be relevant to your trip, such as typhoid and hepatitis A, and check that your travel insurance covers medical care.

## If you still get sick

Rest, sip fluids or oral rehydration solution often, and avoid alcohol. See a doctor for a high fever, blood in your stool, severe or worsening abdominal pain, signs of dehydration, or if you cannot keep fluids down. Learn the [warning signs](https://balibellyrecovery.com/symptoms.html), or see how a [doctor home visit works](https://balibellyrecovery.com/doctor-home-visit.html) if you are too unwell to travel.

## Important note

This article is general information and does not replace an individual medical assessment.
